name: Magnetic moment
seoDesc: Magnetic moment: work out orbital (L) from the spin and the total angular momentum. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Magnetic moment calculator the spin and the total angular momentum and it returns orbital (L). Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Magnetic moment calculator work?
sections.html:
The Magnetic moment calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports orbital (L) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the spin (S) and the total angular momentum (J).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What are the variables at a glance?
sections.html:
Everything the page asks for and everything it reports, side by side. The roles matter: a value you supply is read from the form, a calculated value is derived from the others and cannot be set directly.

FieldWhat it isUnitRole
Spin (S)A plain number, with no unit.—You supply it
Orbital (L)A plain number, with no unit.—Calculated
Total angular momentum (J)A plain number, with no unit.—You supply it
Magnetic momentA number stated in μB.—Calculated

sections.title: The formula behind the Magnetic moment calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Orbital (L)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (-8 × (total angular momentum (J) ^ 2) × g-factor + 12 × (total angular momentum (J) ^ 2) − 8 × total angular momentum (J) × g-factor + 12 × total angular momentum (J) + 4 × (spin (S) ^ 2) + 4 × spin (S) + 1) − 1 ÷ 2
Magnetic moment=g-factor × the square root of (total angular momentum (J) × (total angular momentum (J) + 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Spin (S) = 10, Total angular momentum (J) = 10 and g-factor = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Orbital (L) = -0.5 and Magnetic moment = 104.8809.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Orbital (L) = -0.5 and Magnetic moment = 104.8809 should be roughly the size you expected from Spin (S) = 10 and Total angular momentum (J) = 10.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Magnetic moment calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the spin and the total angular momentum — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Magnetic moment calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — spin for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Magnetic moment calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns orbital (L), derived from the spin and the total angular momentum. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Magnetic moment calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the spin and the total angular momentum, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Orbital (L) = -0.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Magnetic moment calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
